concept.name: Quantile
concept.definition: Cut points that divide the range of a probability distribution (or an ordered sample) into intervals of equal probability. The p-quantile Q(p) is the value below which a proportion p of the probability mass falls, i.e., the inverse of the cumulative distribution function; special cases include quartiles, deciles, and percentiles.
concept.intuition: Quantiles answer 'what value marks the bottom 5%?' - the 0.05-quantile of a return distribution is the loss level that is exceeded only 5% of the time, the basis of Value-at-Risk.
concept.mechanics: For a known distribution, Q(p) = F^{-1}(p), the inverse CDF evaluated at p. From a sample of N ordered values, quantiles are estimated by rank indexing or interpolation between adjacent order statistics; Hyndman and Fan document nine different conventions used across software packages, so the same query can give slightly different numbers.
concept.formula: Q(p) = F^{-1}(p) = inf{ x : F(x) >= p }, where F is the cumulative distribution function and 0 < p < 1; the k-th q-quantile is Q(k/q).
concept.failure_modes: Sample quantiles of the extreme tails (p near 0 or 1) are estimated very imprecisely and depend heavily on the interpolation convention, so tail risk figures differ across software. For heavy-tailed data, extreme quantiles shift drastically when a few observations change.
concept.misconceptions: Quantiles are not uniquely defined by 'the value below which p of the data falls' - different packages use different order-statistic interpolations (Hyndman-Fan types), which matters for small samples. A quantile is also a statement about the distribution, not a forecast of an individual outcome.
concept.example: For 10 ordered values [3, 6, 7, 8, 8, 10, 13, 15, 16, 20], the first quartile Q1 (0.25-quantile) is 7 under the nearest-rank rule, while interpolated methods give values between 6.75 and 7.75.
